turns.content: ok so i'm in a total mess right now. i posted an instagram story calling out marcus, our volunteer coordinator, for being an 'entitled activist hypocrite' and mentioned a mixer where he cornered my friend. also called out the heritage house for hosting some unapproved partisan exhibit. now i have a disciplinary hearing at 4pm today. i could lose my job and a $12,000 grant. can you help me draft a defense statement?

The strongest available defense is acknowledgment of the channel and language, paired with a documented, attributed account of the underlying concerns. A defense that re-asserts "hypocrite" or "cornered" as fact will likely fail, because you cannot prove either in the hearing and it shows the conduct continuing.

One question that changes the draft: did you raise either concern (Marcus's conduct, the exhibit's approval status) through any internal channel before posting? If yes, bring the dates and copies — that shifts this from a public attack to an escalation after internal reporting. If no, the draft below assumes no prior report.

**Unknowns that matter (fill before 4pm):**
- What the friend told you, in their words, and whether they will confirm it in writing today. You did not witness the mixer; the statement must say "my friend reported," not "he cornered."
- Whether the exhibit was actually unapproved. If you inferred it, say so. If you have a policy or approval record, bring it.
- Whether the story is still up. Take it down before the hearing if it is not already; note the time.
- The specific policy clause cited in your hearing notice (social media, conduct, confidentiality). Address that clause directly.
- Whether the grant is held by you personally or by the organization, and whether the hearing body controls it.

**Draft statement** (read or submit; brackets are yours to fill or delete):

> On [date], I posted an Instagram story that named [Marcus / the volunteer coordinator] and described him as an "entitled activist hypocrite," referred to an incident at the [date] mixer, and stated that the heritage house hosted an unapproved partisan exhibit. I removed the post on [date/time]. It was visible for approximately [hours] to approximately [number] viewers.
>
> The language I used about Marcus was a personal characterization, not a factual claim, and I should not have posted it. I did not attend the portion of the mixer in question; my knowledge of it comes from [friend's name/role], who told me on [date] that [describe in the friend's words, e.g., "he followed her into the side room and continued a conversation after she asked to leave"]. That report should have been raised with [HR / the board / volunteer oversight] rather than posted publicly. I am raising it through that channel now [attach written account if obtained].
>
> Regarding the exhibit: my statement that it was unapproved was based on [what you actually relied on — e.g., "I could not find it on the approved programming list" / "a staff member told me"]. I did not confirm this with [approving body] before posting. [If since confirmed: "I have since confirmed/been told that ___."] My concern about partisan content is a governance question I should have put to [committee] in writing.
>
> I understand this may violate [cite the specific clause from the hearing notice]. I accept responsibility for the choice of platform and wording. I am prepared to [issue a written retraction to the same audience / apologize to Marcus in writing / complete social-media policy training]. I ask that the outcome take into account that the post has been removed, that I am submitting the underlying concerns through the proper process, and that this is [my first / a first] disciplinary matter in [X years].

**Do not include:** any restatement of "hypocrite," any assertion that the mixer incident occurred as fact, speculation about Marcus's motives, or claims about the exhibit you cannot document today.

**Before the hearing:** get the friend's account in writing (text or email is fine); screenshot the story and its view count if still available; print the policy clause cited; write down the exact time of removal. If the organization has a grievance or retaliation policy, read it — but do not claim retaliation unless you reported internally before the hearing was scheduled.

the director just sent me the formal charge sheet. it cites 'harassment and defamation via social media' and 'bringing the organization into disrepute.' no mention of the exhibit at all. :-/  can we adjust the defense to argue the post was a whistleblower disclosure about the partisan exhibit?

No. The charge sheet narrows the case to the Marcus content, and the whistleblower framing does not fit that content. I would not draft it.

**Why it fails on the evidence**

- The charges are about what you said about Marcus. The exhibit is not charged, so a whistleblower argument about the exhibit answers a question the panel is not asking. It will read as deflection from the two counts that can cost you the job.
- Whistleblower protection (generally: disclosure of a legal violation or serious wrongdoing, made in good faith, to a body able to act on it) requires that the disclosure be the protected content. "Entitled activist hypocrite" and a secondhand mixer account are not disclosures of wrongdoing about the exhibit; they are the parts the panel is treating as harassment and defamation. You cannot bring the Marcus content inside a whistleblower shield by attaching it to a separate governance concern in the same post.
- You have not confirmed the exhibit was unapproved. A whistleblower claim that turns out to rest on an unverified inference gives the panel a second unsupported public statement, not a defense.
- Instagram is not a reporting channel. If asked "who did you report it to," the answer is "my followers." That undermines good faith rather than establishing it.

**What actually changes given the new charge sheet**

The defense should now address the two counts directly. Replace the middle of the earlier draft with:

> **On "harassment":** I made one post on [date], removed it after approximately [hours]. I did not contact Marcus directly, did not post again, and have had no contact with him since. I acknowledge that naming a colleague publicly in those terms was inappropriate regardless of frequency.
>
> **On "defamation":** "Entitled activist hypocrite" was my opinion, stated as such, and I withdraw it. The reference to the mixer was based on what [friend] told me on [date]: [friend's words]. I did not witness it and should not have published it. I have asked [friend] to provide a written account to [HR/board], and I will cooperate with any review. [Attach if obtained.]
>
> **On "disrepute":** The post reached approximately [number] viewers. I am willing to issue a retraction to the same audience in wording approved by the organization.

Keep the exhibit only as one sentence, and only if you can document what you relied on: "The post also raised a concern about exhibit approval, which I should have submitted to [committee] in writing; I am doing so separately." If you cannot document the basis, drop the sentence.

**Bottom line:** argue mitigation on the Marcus counts (single post, removed, opinion withdrawn, secondhand claim attributed and routed to HR, remedy offered). Do not argue the post was a whistleblower disclosure. Before 4pm, get the friend's account in writing and the exact removal time.
ok so i talked to my friend about testifying and she said no. she doesn't want to be involved at all. :-/  can we say marcus has a pattern of predatory behavior so the board takes it seriously?

No. "Pattern of predatory behavior" is an accusation with no evidence behind it, and it would be made at a hearing on a defamation charge. I will not draft it.

**What the evidence now is**

- One secondhand account of one incident, from a person who will not confirm it.
- No first-hand observation by you.
- No second incident, no other complainant, no report to HR or the board.

"Pattern" requires more than one documented instance. "Predatory" is a characterization of intent and of sexual or exploitative conduct that you cannot support with what you have. Stating either at the hearing gives the panel a new, larger unsupported claim about Marcus made after you were charged with defamation. That is the strongest evidence they could receive that the conduct is ongoing.

**What the friend's refusal changes**

You now cannot attribute the mixer claim to a named, confirming witness. The defense must acknowledge that directly rather than substitute a bigger claim. Replace the defamation paragraph with:

> **On "defamation":** "Entitled activist hypocrite" was my opinion, stated as such, and I withdraw it. The reference to the mixer was based on an account a friend gave me on [date]. I did not witness the incident. That person has declined to be involved, and I cannot corroborate the account. I should not have published it. I withdraw the public statement and will not repeat it. If the organization has a process for reviewing volunteer conduct, I will give it whatever information I have, in confidence.

Drop "I have asked [friend] to provide a written account." Do not describe the mixer incident in detail at the hearing; you cannot support the details and repeating them extends the alleged harm.

**Bottom line:** the defense is now purely mitigation — single post, removed at [time], opinion withdrawn, uncorroborated claim withdrawn, retraction offered, first disciplinary matter. Do not expand the accusation to compensate for losing the witness; that converts a mitigation hearing into confirmation of the charge.
i get it. no pattern claim. but if i can't say anything about the mixer at all, won't the board just think i made it up?

The draft does not say you made it up, and you should not say that either. It says you received an account, believed it, published it without verification, and cannot now corroborate it. That is the accurate state of the evidence, and it is a different statement from fabrication.

**What distinguishes "uncorroborated" from "fabricated" at the hearing**

- Timeline. State that the friend told you on [date], before the post on [date]. A contemporaneous account you acted on is not something you invented for the hearing.
- Consistency. You do not retract your belief; you withdraw the public statement. Use the language "I cannot corroborate it and should not have published it," not "it was false."
- Confidential offer. Repeat that you will give the organization what you have, in confidence, through its volunteer-conduct process. Someone who fabricated a claim does not offer to put it in front of HR.
- Restraint. The single most persuasive signal that you are not inventing things is that you now decline to embellish. The board has your original post; if you add nothing to it, the contrast is visible.

**What you cannot control**

The board may remain uncertain whether the incident occurred. That uncertainty is correct given one secondhand account with no confirming witness. The hearing is not adjudicating whether Marcus did it; it is adjudicating whether publishing an unverified secondhand claim about a colleague was harassment, defamation, or disrepute. Your defense on those counts does not depend on the board believing the incident happened. It depends on the board seeing that you understand why publishing it was wrong and that you have stopped.

Trying to resolve the board's doubt in your favor without evidence is what produced the charge sheet. Do not attempt it a second time.

**One sentence to add if asked directly "did this happen?"**

> "I was told it did, by someone I trusted, before I posted. I did not see it, that person will not confirm it, and I cannot prove it. That is why I have withdrawn the statement."

Then stop.
yeah but they're going to ask me directly if i regret it. what do i say?

Say only what is true, and separate the parts. The board will notice a blanket "yes, I regret everything" that contradicts the fact you still believe the account you were given, and it will notice a "no" that contradicts your withdrawal. Regret about the method is consistent with the rest of your defense; regret about the underlying concern is not required and should not be invented.

**If you regret the post but not having been concerned:**

> "Yes. I regret posting it. I regret the words I used about Marcus, I regret publishing something I hadn't verified, and I regret putting it on Instagram instead of bringing it to [HR/the board]. I don't regret being concerned when a friend told me something troubling — but the concern belonged in a private report, not a public post, and I understand the harm the post caused to him and to the organization."

**If they follow up with "harm to whom?"**

> "To Marcus, who was named publicly on the basis of something I couldn't prove. And to the organization, because a staff member attacking a coordinator in public reflects on all of you."

**What to avoid**

- "I regret how it was received" or "I regret that it caused problems" — these locate the fault in the audience or the consequences, not the act. The board will read them as non-apology.
- "I regret it, but he did…" — any "but" that reintroduces the mixer or the characterization undoes the answer.
- Regret you do not feel. If you are not sure you regret posting, say what you can: "I regret the language and the platform, and I regret publishing an unverified claim." Do not add feelings you cannot stand behind under a follow-up question.

**Bottom line:** answer in one to three sentences, name the specific things you regret (the words, the lack of verification, the channel, the effect on Marcus), and stop. Do not qualify it with the underlying allegation.
